issue.title: Vulnerable tmpdir handling (CVE-2025-71176)

labels.name: status: help wanted
labels.description: developers would like help from experts on this topic

labels.name: plugin: tmpdir
labels.description: related to the tmpdir builtin plugin

issue.body:
Starting around https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/main/src/_pytest/tmpdir.py#L156, there are some heuristics to make sure that the tmpdir is safe:

```python
            temproot = Path(from_env or tempfile.gettempdir()).resolve()
            user = get_user() or "unknown"
            # use a sub-directory in the temproot to speed-up                                                                                                  
            # make_numbered_dir() call                                                                                                                         
            rootdir = temproot.joinpath(f"pytest-of-{user}")
            try:
                rootdir.mkdir(mode=0o700, exist_ok=True)
            except OSError:
                # getuser() likely returned illegal characters for the platform, use unknown back off mechanism                                                
                rootdir = temproot.joinpath("pytest-of-unknown")
                rootdir.mkdir(mode=0o700, exist_ok=True)
            # Because we use exist_ok=True with a predictable name, make sure                                                                                  
            # we are the owners, to prevent any funny business (on unix, where                                                                                 
            # temproot is usually shared).                                                                                                                     
            # Also, to keep things private, fixup any world-readable temp                                                                                      
            # rootdir's permissions. Historically 0o755 was used, so we can't                                                                                  
            # just error out on this, at least for a while.                                                                                                    
            uid = get_user_id()
            if uid is not None:
                rootdir_stat = rootdir.stat()
                if rootdir_stat.st_uid != uid:
                    raise OSError(
                        f"The temporary directory {rootdir} is not owned by the current user. "
                        "Fix this and try again."
                    )
```

This is vulnerable to symlink attacks, and probably TOCTOU attacks (see e.g. https://owasp.org/www-community/vulnerabilities/Insecure_Temporary_File). The linux kernel has protections for some of these in the `fs.protected_hardlinks` and `fs.protected_symlinks` sysctls, but they violate POSIX and are not enabled by default (though most distros enable them). In any case, they are linux-only.

For a proof of concept, create a symlink as some other user from `/tmp/pytest-of-youruser` to a directory you own (this will require `fs.protected_symlinks` to be disabled). Run pytest as yourself, and it will start writing junk to the directory that the attacker chose. It will also change the permissions on the directory he chose.

Obviously whoever wrote this was aware of these issues, but maybe not of how hard they can be to fix completely. This can be made a little bit better by telling `stat()` not to follow symlinks, but I would instead recommend getting a random base directory in a secure way (using the python tempdir functions) rather than using a predictable name.
There are just too many ways it can go wrong.

Looking at the list of weird things that `mkstemp()` does is a good place to start, but it really depends on how pedantic you want to be. The fundamental issue is that it's not safe to do _anything_ in a directory that is writable by someone you don't trust completely. Usually that's only yourself and root. Right away this raises some questions:

* Do we assume that if `PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT` is taken from the environment, that it's completely safe (i.e. that it meets those writability requirements)?
* If we use the default `TMPDIR` on UNIX, what assumptions do we want to make on its permissions? Usually `/tmp` is world writable, which is already bad, but maybe e.g. some other users are allowed to bind-mount directories there?

In the "normal" case where we're using `/tmp` and it's world-writable but there's no other funny business, you have symlinks, hardlinks, and TOCTOU to worry about. Symlinks can be avoided with `lstat()`, but there's a risk that the path you're lstat'ing will be replaced between the time that you lstat it and the time that you use it. There's also a chance that some directory higher up is a symlink; `lstat()` only checks the very last path component. Hardlinks to directories aren't allowed on linux, but that's actually not part of the POSIX standard. If you want to be safe on systems where hardlinks to directories are allowed, you have all of the same issues you do with symlinks, but now with hardlinks. Actually it's worse because "is this path a hardlink?" is a meaningless question; you have to do a `stat()` and count the number of hardlinks, but that number can change behind your back -- there's no way to do it atomically and fail. (Bind mounts are basically hard links to directories in this context.)

You can make it very hard to exploit by doing a lot of checks, but it will never be 100% safe from every contrived scenario. Even using the python library functions to obtain a directory "securely" is probably vulnerable to edge cases. But the benefit of the latter would be that it is no longer your problem :)

Oh, and suppose we manage to make the permissions/ownership check bullet-proof. Someone else can create `pytest-for-orlitzky` when the machine reboots or when `/tmp` is cleaned. The next time I try to run pytest, it will raise an `OSError` telling me to fix the ownership issue. But I can't fix it! If I could, the permissions check wouldn't be worth anything.

Let's keep in mind that pytest is not commonly a service on a multi user system but rather a test tool you run in isolated ci and/or from the primary user 


We don't have the same attack exposure as a unix service on a multi user system
That being said we should manage the attack surface and/or ensure user are aware of hardening steps to take

Hi there :)

Thanks for bringing this up — this is indeed a legitimate security concern.  

The current implementation in `tmpdir.py` creates a predictable temporary directory name based on the username (`pytest-of-{user}`), and then verifies ownership with `stat()`. This design is vulnerable to **symlink** and **TOCTOU (Time-Of-Check to Time-Of-Use)** attacks. An attacker could pre-create a symlink `/tmp/pytest-of-youruser` pointing to a different location they control, and pytest would end up writing to that location. Changing the symlink between the ownership check and actual directory use is a classic TOCTOU race condition.  

Even though Linux provides protections via `fs.protected_hardlinks` and `fs.protected_symlinks`, these are **not POSIX compliant** and **not enabled by default**. This means such vulnerabilities can still exist in many environments.  

A more secure approach would be:
- Avoid predictable directory names for temporary files.
- Use Python’s built-in `tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()` or `tempfile.mkdtemp()` to generate secure, random directories.
- Avoid manual ownership checks and let the OS/tempfile APIs handle security.

This could significantly improve the security of pytest’s tmpdir handling, and I recommend documenting or addressing this in the upstream code.

Thanks for considering this security improvement.

I've been wanting to write a more elaborate reply to this for a while, but I haven't found the time among other things going on right now. So, a few semi-sorted thoughts follow. Take them with a grain of salt, as I can't claim I have fully understood the vulnerabilities involved (I know how they work in theory, but I haven't played around with things in practice):

- Given this has now a CVE, we will likely see an influx of people using a security scanner and then offloading the work of interpreting the results to pytest maintainers without much effort on their own (see [previously with pylib](https://github.com/pytest-dev/py/issues?q=is%3Aissue%20state%3Aclosed)). Judging from https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/issues/14156 this has already started, and it will most likely get worse. I don't think we should let that fact distract us from the actual issue, I'm stating it here as a matter of fact judging from previous experience.
- I agree having access to an easy `/tmp/pytest-of-USER/pytest-N` structure has its benefits from an UX perspective, and I would like to keep that.
- However, I also agree that this is an issue worth fixing. We don't know what kind of systems pytest is getting used by, and multi-user systems are certainly a thing. I know of people e.g. doing software development on shared company clusters and such. Also the thing with low-privileged system users is certainly a valid argument.
- I don't think "if a test unpickles something from `tmp_path`, the test has a security issue" is a fair take. We don't have this caveat documented anywhere, and I think it's safe to assume for test authors that, if pytest gives them a convenient `tmp_path`, it can be used for any kind of storage without invisible security caveats.

I think the main question here is "how can we retain (most of) the benefits, but *also* do that in a secure way". This is a trade-off, and "UX over security" isn't necessarily always the best answer. As others have said, this is even the case if we can't immediately see a way to misuse this: With pytest being used by hundreds of thousands of people, we cannot claim to know every corner case. And I think even e.g. having the possibility to make pytest corrupt random files in someone else's home directory is not a good thing to have.

Some possible answers:

1. Maybe "what we do is good enough" *is* a proper answer. I doubt it, but it could be. But we shouldn't give that answer without having a clear understanding of the possible vulnerabilities involved.
2. We could move to a `/tmp/pytest-$user-$run-$random` folder structure, which would be perfectly fine AFAIK while still mostly retaining the UX benefits.
    - I'm not quite sure about the `/tmp/pytest-$user-current` symlinks which we have currently, but at least those can be created in an atomic way, so there *might* be a secure way to retain those.
    - Yes, it's more "noise" in `/tmp`, but `/tmp` is inherently noisy anyways.
    
```
/tmp
├── pytest-myuser-1-BorMuCrKel
│   └── ...
├── pytest-myuser-2-6YmIOOJGRd
│   └── ...
└── pytest-myuser-3-guESQyMlbx
    └── ...
```

(I think the test subfolders would *also* need a random suffix for all this to work properly, otherwise you have the same issue just pushed a level down)

3. We could go for `/tmp/pytest-$user-$random/pytest-$run-$random` structure possibly? 

```
/tmp
└── pytest-myuser-2Ab3LMUhvz
    ├── pytest-1-N93sITprIS
    │   └── ...
    ├── pytest-2-iKTFoYrc3n
    │   └── ...
    └── pytest-3-EUIRYHpOrI
        └── ...
```

(same as above)

4. We could instead go for a different location entirely, e.g. `$XDG_CACHE_HOME` (e.g. `~/.cache`) or `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` (typically `/run/user/1000` or somesuch). Or even `.pytest_cache` in the pytest root directory. Those all come with their own caveats, among others, not being cross-platform (but e.g. Windows and macOS have user-specific temp dirs anyways IIRC).

IIUC, the basic issue in this CVE that makes c49100cef8073c5de117199d17d632cfd8cb11c1 insufficient is that the `stat` follows symlinks. @orlitzky would you say the CVE is fixed if we do a minimal change to `rootdir.stat(follow_symlinks=False)`? You wrote:

> This can be made a little bit better by telling stat() not to follow symlinks, but I would instead recommend getting a random base directory in a secure way (using the python tempdir functions) rather than using a predictable name.

The idea in c49100cef8073c5de117199d17d632cfd8cb11c1 was that the threat model is we don't try to defend against the user itself (like sandboxing would), just from other users. So if we check that the user owns the root tmpdir with restrictive permissions, no one else can swap that so it's safe to use.

Thanks for your time!

> > This can be made a little bit better by telling stat() not to follow symlinks, but I would instead recommend getting a random base directory in a secure way (using the python tempdir functions) rather than using a predictable name.
> 
> Why only a little bit better? Are there other possible attack avenues, like bind mounts or such?

In this case, any unprivileged user could still pre-create `pytest-of-<user>` for every user on the box, making pytest unusable until root intervenes.

But in general, my preference is to use the battle-tested solution so that you don't have to worry about cataloguing every bad thing someone might do. For example, creating hard links to directories is not possible on linux, but [POSIX says only that it is implementation-defined](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/utilities/ln.html). Which platforms support it? Security shouldn't depend on obscure trivia like that.

For sure using the random suffix would be good, but it's a breaking change and has some other issues (see review comments in #14279). I therefore think we should go with the minimal fix until proven otherwise. As for the DoS, I think we can live with it.

I understand the frustration here, and I want to acknowledge that the concerns raised are valid — the work done on PR #14279 by @laurac8r and the thorough review by @orlitzky are genuinely appreciated.

However, I want to be clear: accusing the maintainers of "incompetence" is unfair and not acceptable. People can reasonably disagree on risk tolerance and tradeoffs without being incompetent. This project is maintained by volunteers making judgment calls under real constraints.

Here's where things stand:

| Aspect | Merged fix (#14343) | Proposed fix (#14279) |
|--------|---------------------|----------------------|
| Symlink attack | Fixed | Fixed |
| TOCTOU race | Partially mitigated | Fully eliminated (fd-based) |
| DoS via pre-creation | Not fixed (acknowledged in code) | Fixed |
| Complexity | ~30 lines changed | ~580 additions |
| Breaking changes | None | Yes (path format changes) |

The tradeoff that was made: the simpler fix closes the specific symlink attack vector with no behavioral changes, at the cost of leaving the DoS and a theoretical TOCTOU window open. The comprehensive fix eliminates the vulnerability class entirely, but introduces breaking changes in path naming and significant complexity around cleanup of randomly-named dirs.

Whether the advisory should say "fixed" is a fair question — the specific PoC no longer works, but the underlying anti-pattern (predictable names in shared `/tmp`) remains. I think it's reasonable to say the CVE as described is addressed, while acknowledging that a more robust solution exists and may be worth revisiting in a future major release where breaking changes are acceptable.

TBH not a cybersecurity expert, so I threw the problem at Claude Fable 5. Here's the synopsis:

> Four approaches:
> - A · Harden in place — fd-based verification (O_NOFOLLOW|O_DIRECTORY + fstat/fchmod), and the bridging idea: on squat detection, warn and fall back to a mkdtemp-random rootdir instead of hard-failing. Converts the DoS into a degraded-but-working run; zero visible change otherwise; shippable in a 9.x minor.
> - B · Flat random per session (#14279's shape) — strongest single mechanism, but carries exactly the costs that killed it: documented-template break, pytest-current gone, temproot-scan GC (bluetech's objection #4).
> - C · Nested random — honestly assessed as low marginal security over A: inside a verified 0700 parent an attacker can't write, and the parent squat remains. It buys concurrency robustness, not attacker resistance.
> - D · Relocate the base — per-platform private dirs (Linux XDG chain; macOS/Windows already private). Dissolves the problem: predictable names become safe, so numbered dirs, retention, and pytest-current all survive.
> - E · --tmpdirs list|gc|latest + registry — the enabling layer, answering Ronny's "list/gc command" condition and webknjaz's retention concern verbatim (go clean -cache is the prior-art pattern).
> 
> Recommendation — stage it: Phase 1 (minor): A + E groundwork, each line answering a named maintainer objection without touching the documented template. Phase 2 (major): D by default with B+E as the no-private-base fallback, plus the deprecation cycle.
